blocks.content: FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Right to Equality covers Articles 14 to 18.
Right to Freedom is detailed under Articles 19 to 22.
Right against Exploitation is protected under Articles 23 and 24.
Freedom of Religion is enshrined under Articles 25 through 28.
Cultural and Educational Rights are provided in Articles 29 and 30.
Article 32 empowers citizens with the Right to Constitutional Remedies through Writs.

blocks.content: Fundamental Rights are the basic human rights guaranteed to all citizens of India by the Constitution. These rights are essential for the development of an individual and for the functioning of a democratic society.
Fundamental Rights are mentioned in Part III of the Indian Constitution (Articles 12 to 35). They protect citizens from arbitrary actions of the State and ensure equality, liberty, and justice.
FEATURES OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS

items:
• Guaranteed by the Constitution
  • Justiciable in nature (enforceable by courts)
  • Available to citizens and in some cases to foreigners
  • Not absolute – subject to reasonable restrictions
  • Can be suspended during National Emergency (except Articles 20 and 21)
Available to citizens and in some cases to foreigners
Not absolute – subject to reasonable restrictions
Can be suspended during National Emergency (except Articles 20 and 21)

blocks.content: CLASSIFICATION OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS
Fundamental Rights are classified into six categories:
RIGHT TO EQUALITY (ARTICLES 14–18)
This right ensures equality before law and equal protection of laws.
Article 14 – Equality before law and equal protection of laws Article 15 – Prohibition of discrimination
Article 16 – Equality of opportunity in public employment Article 17 – Abolition of untouchability
Article 18 – Abolition of titles
This right establishes political and social equality.
RIGHT TO FREEDOM (ARTICLES 19–22)
Article 19 guarantees six freedoms:
Article 20 provides protection in respect of conviction for offences. Article 21 guarantees protection of life and personal liberty.
Article 22 provides protection against arbitrary arrest and detention. Article 21 is the heart of the Constitution.

blocks.content: RIGHT TO FREEDOM OF RELIGION (ARTICLES 25–28)
This right ensures religious freedom to all citizens.
Article 25 – Freedom of conscience and religion Article 26 – Manage religious affairs
Article 27 – No tax for promotion of religion Article 28 – Freedom from religious instruction
India is a secular country.
CULTURAL AND EDUCATIONAL RIGHTS (ARTICLES 29–30)
These rights protect the culture of minorities.
Article 29 – Protection of language, script and culture
Article 30 – Right of minorities to establish educational institutions These rights promote unity in diversity.
RIGHT TO CONSTITUTIONAL REMEDIES (ARTICLE 32)
Article 32 is called the „Heart and Soul of the Constitution‟ by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
It empowers citizens to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Writs:
WRITS – EXPLANATION
Habeas Corpus – To protect personal liberty Mandamus – Order to perform duty
Prohibition – Stops lower court from acting beyond power Certiorari – Quashes illegal orders
Quo Warranto – Questions authority of a person
REASONABLE RESTRICTIONS
Fundamental Rights are not absolute. Restrictions can be imposed in the interest of:

items:
• Public order
  • Morality
  • Security of state
  • Friendly relations with foreign states
Article 32 is crucial for competitive exams as it details Constitutional Remedies and Writs.
Distinguish clearly between the Article ranges: Right to Equality (14–18) vs. Right to Freedom (19–22).
Pay special attention to the Suspension of Fundamental Rights and Important Supreme Court Judgments.

blocks.content: SUSPENSION OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS
During National Emergency:

items:
• Article 19 can be suspended
  • Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended

blocks.content: IMPORTANCE OF FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS

items:
• Protect individual liberty
  • Promote democracy
  • Ensure equality
  • Protect minorities
  • Strengthen rule of law

blocks.content: CONCLUSION

Fundamental Rights form the backbone of Indian democracy. They ensure freedom, equality and justice for citizens. These rights protect individuals from arbitrary state actions and promote a just and inclusive society.
